ON.summary: Ontario private well owners can have their water tested for bacteria free of charge through Public Health Ontario (PHO) laboratories: pick up a sample kit from a PHO lab, the local public health unit or one of its designated pickup locations, then drop the sample back off (results are available through PHO's online Water Testing Portal). PHO tests only for the indicator bacteria E. coli and total coliforms; chemical testing (e.g., nitrate, sodium, metals) must go to a licensed private laboratory, which charges a fee. The provincial fact sheet only says to test regularly, while local health units (e.g., Ottawa, Durham, York, Halton, Hamilton, Waterloo Region) recommend at least three times a year: spring, summer and fall.
ON.cost: Free for bacterial testing through PHO. Chemical testing at licensed private labs is fee-based (the province does not publish prices). Some health units add extras: Halton Region tests nitrate free; Region of Waterloo charges $21.40 each for nitrate or fluoride tests.
ON.tests: Free PHO test: indicator bacteria only (total coliforms and E. coli). No chemical testing.
ON.frequency: Province: test 'regularly' (no fixed schedule; more testing after spring melt and unusual events). Local health units: at least 3 times a year (spring, summer, fall), plus after flooding, heavy rain or well work.
ON.bottles: Free kits from PHO laboratories, local public health units and their designated pickup locations (regional offices, libraries, municipal offices, some rural stores); Halton also mails bottles on request.
ON.notes: Ontario's Auditor General (2025, reported by CBC) estimated about 1.3 million Ontarians rely on private wells and fewer than one-third had tested in the previous 12 months. A 2023 AG report said PHO had proposed a 'gradual discontinuation' of free private water testing; the Health Minister said in 2024 it would be kept, and PHO was still promoting free testing in June 2026.

QC.summary: Quebec has no free provincial testing service for private wells: owners send samples to a laboratory accredited by the Environment ministry (list kept by the CEAEQ, which itself does not test water for individuals), and the lab supplies the sample containers and instructions. The ministry recommends a microbiological analysis (E. coli, enterococci, total coliforms) at least twice a year, in spring and fall, and a physico-chemical analysis (arsenic, manganese, barium, nitrates-nitrites, chlorides, sodium, iron, sulfates, fluorides, hardness) at least once while the well is in use, plus nitrates-nitrites every spring and fall in farm areas or where homes have individual septic systems.
QC.cost: Paid by the owner; the CEAEQ lab list states analyses are a paid service priced by each lab. A provincially funded guide (moneaumonpuits.ca) says to expect from a few tens to a few hundred dollars per analysis, depending on the tests.
QC.tests: Microbiological: E. coli, enterococci, total coliforms. Physico-chemical (at least once): arsenic, manganese, barium, nitrates-nitrites, chlorides, sodium, iron, sulfates, fluorides, total hardness.
QC.frequency: Microbiological at least twice a year (spring and fall); physico-chemical at least once during the period the well is used; nitrates-nitrites each spring and fall in agricultural areas or where septic systems are individual.
QC.bottles: From the accredited laboratory you choose (ministry leaflet); moneaumonpuits.ca adds that the municipality may also provide them.

BC.summary: We found no free public testing program for private wells in B.C.: HealthLinkBC tells owners to use a qualified laboratory (searchable in the CALA directory), which provides the sample bottles and instructions, and the lab charges for the analysis. It recommends bacteriological testing (total coliforms and E. coli) at least once a year, or immediately if clarity, colour or taste changes, and chemical testing when well construction is complete and annually after that. HealthLinkBC names nitrates, fluoride and metals such as arsenic, lead, copper and manganese as the most common chemicals of concern in B.C. groundwater.
BC.cost: Fee paid to the private lab; no provincial price published. Some local governments subsidize tests (e.g., the Regional District of Nanaimo rebates 50% of a qualifying test, up to $350).
BC.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry packages chosen with the lab (nitrate, fluoride, metals such as arsenic, lead, copper, manganese).
BC.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year (and immediately after changes in clarity, colour or taste); chemistry when the well is completed and annually thereafter.
BC.notes: No provincial free-testing program was found; local programs exist in some areas (RDN rebate; Township of Langley Private Well Network lab discount).

AB.summary: Alberta Health Services (AHS) Environmental Public Health tests water from private drinking-water supplies (wells, cisterns, surface water) free of charge: a bacteria test (total coliforms and E. coli) and a chemical and trace-metals test. Bottles are picked up and dropped off at AHS facilities (listed on InformAlberta); AHS will not test samples collected for real-estate, commercial or agricultural purposes, or municipal tap water. MyHealth Alberta advises testing for bacteria 2 times a year and for chemicals and trace metals every 3 years.
AB.cost: Free: AHS describes it as a free service (2015 AHS release); the current AHS and MyHealth Alberta pages describe the service without listing any fee.
AB.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); routine chemistry (pH, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, hardness, TDS, iron, alkalinity, chloride, fluoride, nitrite/nitrate, sulphate); trace metals (e.g., arsenic, lead, manganese).
AB.frequency: Bacteria 2 times a year; chemicals and trace metals every 3 years.
AB.bottles: AHS facilities/community health centres; see InformAlberta's 'Environmental Public Health - Water Sample Bottle Pick-up & Drop-off' listing.
AB.notes: AHS pick-up listings note the lab will not accept samples taken more than 24 hours before they arrive (e.g., Strathcona County Health Centre listing: https://www.albertahealthservices.ca/findhealth/Service.aspx?id=1083627&serviceAtFacilityID=1132297).

SK.summary: Saskatchewan well owners can have their water tested for a fee at the Roy Romanow Provincial Laboratory (RRPL, Saskatchewan Health Authority), which distributes sample bottles to rural municipality (RM) offices and public health offices across the province. The SHA advises testing private supplies annually for total coliform bacteria and nitrate. RRPL's published fee schedule (effective April 1, 2017; the lab asks you to confirm current prices) lists $23 for total coliforms/E. coli, $29 for a 'water potability' panel (bacteria plus nitrate) and $104 for a general chemical analysis.
SK.cost: Fee-based (GST included, schedule effective April 1, 2017; confirm at 1-866-450-0000): total coliforms + E. coli $23.00; nitrate $11.50; water potability panel $29.00; general chemical/water quality analysis $104.00; arsenic $23.00.
SK.tests: Bacteriological (total coliforms, E. coli) and chemical tests (nitrate, fluoride, general chemistry panel; individual metals such as arsenic).
SK.frequency: Annually for total coliform bacteria and nitrate.
SK.bottles: RM offices and public health offices (supplied by RRPL), or from RRPL directly.

MB.summary: Manitoba subsidizes rather than provides free testing: its Private Well Testing Subsidy Program gives private well and cistern owners one subsidized bacteria test a year (total coliforms and E. coli) at Duracan Laboratory, 862 Dufferin Ave., Winnipeg, for $17.67 including tax, and a positive result comes with disinfection instructions and a coupon for a free re-test. The province says to test at least once a year, ideally in spring after snowmelt and after flooding or heavy rain. Bottles come from the lab, and some RM offices stock Duracan bottles.
MB.cost: $17.67 (tax included) for the once-a-year subsidized bacteria test; free re-test after a positive result. For flood-affected owners the subsidy was temporarily raised to 100% from June 15 to August 31, 2026. Chemical tests are not covered by the subsidy.
MB.tests: Subsidized test: total coliforms and E. coli.
MB.frequency: At least once a year (spring after snowmelt is ideal); also after flooding, heavy rain or changes in the water.
MB.bottles: From the lab (Duracan); some RM offices (e.g., RM of St. Clements) stock Duracan bottles; the 2019 provincial fact sheet also points to RM and Conservation District offices.
MB.notes: Manitoba publishes fact sheets on naturally occurring nitrate, arsenic, uranium, fluoride, manganese and other elements in well water, but we found no provincial chemistry-testing program.

NS.summary: More than 40% of Nova Scotia households get their drinking water from their own private wells. Owners pay for testing: bottles are picked up and samples dropped off at Nova Scotia Health (NSH) locations around the province (other labs also test drinking water), and NSH charges $34.50 for a total coliform/E. coli presence-absence test and $37.63 to $138.77 for its chemical packages. The province's current guidance is to test at least every year for bacteria and every five years for chemical contaminants, using a list of about 30 parameters that includes arsenic, uranium, lead, manganese, nitrate/nitrite and fluoride.
NS.cost: NSH fees: total coliform & E. coli presence/absence $34.50 (MPN count $46.00); chemical Package A (arsenic, uranium) $37.63, Package B $59.10, Package C $120.67, Package D $138.77.
NS.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry: province lists ~30 parameters (alkalinity, metals incl. arsenic, lead, manganese, uranium; nitrate/nitrite; fluoride; hardness; etc.).
NS.frequency: Bacteria at least every year; chemical contaminants every five years (surface-water supplies: bacteria every six months, chemistry yearly).
NS.bottles: NSH hospitals/health centres and some municipal offices (see the NSH water-testing pick-up/drop-off map).
NS.notes: NSH's water-testing page still cites an older recommendation (bacteria every six months, chemistry every two years); the novascotia.ca page is the current provincial guidance. Several eastern NSH sites currently redirect bacterial samples to Bureau Veritas in Sydney.

NB.summary: New Brunswick well owners pay for testing. RPC Analytical Services is the designated provincial analytical lab (offices in Fredericton and Moncton); water-testing kits with bottles and instructions are available at Service New Brunswick (SNB) offices or RPC, and samples go back to RPC, a designated SNB office or any ISO 17025-accredited lab. The province recommends testing for bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli) twice a year, ideally at spring thaw and during fall rains, and for inorganic contaminants (e.g., arsenic, uranium, fluoride, nitrate) when a well is drilled and every two years after.
NB.cost: Fee-based; prices are not published on the provincial or RPC pages (contact RPC).
NB.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); inorganics (e.g., arsenic, uranium, fluoride, nitrate); organics (petroleum, pesticides, solvents) where there is a specific risk.
NB.frequency: Bacteria twice a year (spring thaw, fall rains); inorganics at drilling and every two years after.
NB.bottles: Designated SNB offices or RPC Analytical Services (Fredericton, Moncton).
NB.notes: SNB offices accept samples only on certain days/mornings, so call ahead.

PE.summary: Since January 1, 2022, Islanders with residential wells can get free bacterial and general-chemistry testing of their drinking water through the provincial PEI Analytical Laboratories. Bottles and forms are available at the lab (23 Innovation Way, Charlottetown) or any Access PEI site, and samples can be dropped at Access PEI centres outside Charlottetown. The province recommends a bacteria test at least once a year and a chemical analysis when a well is first drilled and every 2 years after.
PE.cost: Free for residential wells. Per CBC (2021), the law covers bacteria once every six months and chemistry once every two years; before 2022 the fees were $40 (bacteria) and $95 (chemistry) plus tax.
PE.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli) and general chemistry.
PE.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year; chemistry when the well is drilled and every 2 years after.
PE.bottles: PEI Analytical Laboratories, 23 Innovation Way, Charlottetown, or any Access PEI site.

NL.summary: Newfoundland and Labrador tests private water supplies for bacteria free of charge: sterile bottles are available at Government Service Centre (Digital Government and Service NL) offices and the NL Public Health Laboratory, and samples go to the nearest Government Service Centre or, in St. John's, to the Public Health Laboratory at the Miller Centre. Chemical testing is not free and is done by private laboratories (the province keeps a list of approved labs). A provincial pilot launched in December 2022 handed out free chemistry test kits; we could not confirm whether it is still running.
NL.cost: Bacteriological: no fee. Chemical: private-lab fees (amounts not published).
NL.tests: Free test: total coliforms and E. coli (presence/absence).
NL.bottles: Government Service Centre offices and the NL Public Health Laboratory (Miller Centre, St. John's).
NL.notes: Frequency is null: no provincial testing-frequency recommendation was found on the pages reviewed.

YT.summary: Yukon's Environmental Health Services Water Laboratory (#2 Hospital Road, Whitehorse) tests well water for total coliforms and E. coli at no cost; owners get a sampling bottle and form by visiting the office or calling 867-667-8391 (toll-free 1-800-661-0408 ext. 8391), keep the sample cool and deliver it within 24 hours on the lab's receiving days. No Yukon lab tests drinking water for chemical, physical or radiological parameters, so those tests go to accredited labs in B.C. or Alberta at the owner's cost, often as much as $200 plus shipping for the 30 common parameters. The territory recommends bacteria testing at least once a year and chemistry for two consecutive years at first, then every five years if nothing changes.
YT.cost: Bacteria: free. Chemistry: paid to B.C./Alberta accredited labs, often as much as $200 plus shipping.
YT.tests: Free: total coliforms and E. coli. Chemistry (30 parameters incl. arsenic, uranium, lead, manganese, nitrate, fluoride) at out-of-territory labs.
YT.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year; chemistry 2 consecutive years initially, then every 5 years if no concerns.
YT.bottles: Environmental Health Services, #2 Hospital Road, Whitehorse (in person or by phone); chemistry labs supply their own bottles.

NT.summary: We found no GNWT page describing a testing program or recommended testing schedule for private household wells. Private citizens can use the GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife (Department of Environment and Climate Change), which supplies sampling bottles free (shipping extra). Its July 2021 price guide lists total coliforms + E. coli (drinking water) at $28 per sample and an annual drinking-water chemistry package at $380 per sample, with prices subject to change.
NT.cost: Fee-based at Taiga (2021 price guide: $28 bacteria; $380 annual drinking-water chemistry package); no free program found.
NT.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry packages (metals incl. arsenic, uranium, lead; nitrate; fluoride; etc.).
NT.bottles: Taiga Environmental Laboratory provides sampling supplies free of charge (pick-up in Yellowknife or shipped).
NT.notes: Frequency is null: no NWT recommendation for private wells was found. NCCEH (2013) notes that larger NWT communities have piped and/or trucked water systems, while many smaller settlements have no central water supply.

HRM has also offered drinking water and showers to residents with dry wells during droughts, e.g., 2018 (https://www.halifax.ca/home/news/municipality-helps-residents-well-water-shortages) and 2022.
halifax.note: 2017 estimate (NS Geoscience and Mines Branch, 2016 Census base): 83,586 of 403,391 HRM residents on private wells.

nanaimo.note: The RDN rebate covers all member municipalities; it shows some wells exist in the city but not how many.

yellowknife.sentence: About 680 Yellowknife residents (roughly 4%) receive the City's trucked water and most others are on its piped system, so private household wells are rare.
yellowknife.localProgram: The GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife accepts samples from private citizens (fee-based; bottles free) (https://www.gov.nt.ca/ecc/en/services/taiga-environmental-laboratory).
yellowknife.note: The source (CBC, June 2025, citing a consultants' report) describes piped vs. trucked service, not wells directly.
